analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement tools against employers paying women less than men for the same work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was introduced with 197 cosponsors, all Democrats, sent to committee and a subcommittee, and died there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would toughen the Equal Pay Act, the law against paying women less than men for the same work. It would narrow employers' excuses for pay gaps, let workers collect compensatory and punitive damages, protect employees who ask about or share their own wages, allow equal pay claims to be filed as class actions, and require the government to collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin. It was referred to a committee, then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than similarly situated men, including women in lower-wage jobs where a single lawsuit is not worth the cost. Class-action treatment would let groups of employees band together, and the ban on retaliation would protect workers who ask what their colleagues earn.

how_it_helps.text: The bill limits the employer defense that a pay gap rests on 'any other factor other than sex' to bona fide factors such as education, training, or experience, which must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, and cannot be rooted in a prior sex-based pay difference.

It makes violating employers liable for compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, which the Equal Pay Act's existing remedies largely do not provide.
It protects employees from being fired or punished for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages — their own or another employee's — in connection with a complaint or investigation.
It allows equal pay claims to proceed as class actions without each worker's written consent, so employees at one workplace could join together in a single case.

It would require the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to collect pay information from employers by employees' sex, race, and national origin, giving enforcers the data to find patterns of discrimination.
It authorizes a $15 million grant program for negotiation-skills training for girls and women, and requires the Labor Department and EEOC to develop compliance guidance for small businesses.

It counts employees as being in the same workplace for comparison purposes if they work for the same employer within the same county, making it harder to shield pay gaps by splitting workers across facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have underpaid women would owe compensatory and possibly punitive damages, would face more lawsuits including class actions, and would bear new reporting burdens. Employers with genuinely sex-neutral pay would face mostly paperwork and litigation exposure.

drawbacks.text: The bill would increase litigation costs for employers: unlimited compensatory damages, punitive damages, class actions without individual consent, and comparisons across an entire county rather than a single workplace all raise the stakes of any wage dispute, including ones filed in good faith.

The 'alternative employment practice' clause would let a court order an employer to adopt a different business practice whenever a worker shows another method would serve the same business purpose, which businesses groups said second-guesses legitimate management decisions.

EEOC collection of pay data by sex, race, and national origin imposes new recordkeeping and reporting requirements on employers, though the bill directs the agency to weigh the burden on employers in designing the rules.

The class-action provision means individual employees would lose some say in whether and how a claim on their behalf is settled, since the bill removes the written-consent requirement for equal pay class actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing real pay discrimination, the bill closes loopholes that have made the Equal Pay Act hard to enforce and adds remedies that actually compensate the harmed. The cost falls on employers in the form of higher damages exposure, more litigation, and new data reporting, and honest supporters would acknowledge the county-wide comparison standard and the alternative-practice clause broaden cases beyond the original law. The compliance guidance for small businesses, an exemption matching the Fair Labor Standards Act's small-firm threshold, and a $15 million budget modestly soften the burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act on April 13, 2011, with 197 cosponsors.
All 197 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced.
On May 20, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and that was the last recorded action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill never reached the House floor and never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new damages liability, class-action exposure, and pay-data reporting are better off because the bill never advanced; the House leadership and committee majority that kept it off the agenda preserved the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: All 197 cosponsors were Democrats, none of the House's 240-plus Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would expose employers that underpay women to compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and EEOC pay-data reporting by sex, race, and national origin. Business groups opposed the bill, arguing it would drive litigation, and the House leadership that would not schedule it faced this pressure.

Contractors would have faced reinstated equal-opportunity surveys and broader investigative methods at the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs for pay discrimination cases. The added scrutiny targets pay gaps that affect workers.

industries.industry: Small businesses below the Fair Labor Standards Act coverage threshold
industries.note: The bill exempts small businesses to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and requires agencies to produce compliance guidance for them, sparing the smallest firms new liability and paperwork.
